items.title: Global landmine casualties hit a five-year high, driven by Myanmar, Syria
items.summary:
Global landmine casualties hit a five-year high, driven by Myanmar, Syria
Landmine monitor found 84 percent of deaths caused by landmines were in Southeast Asia.
Casualties from landmines or unexploded ordnance reached a five-year high in 2025, with the largest number of deaths recorded in Southeast
items.text:
Global landmine casualties hit a five-year high, driven by Myanmar, Syria
Landmine monitor found 84 percent of deaths caused by landmines were in Southeast Asia.
Casualties from landmines or unexploded ordnance reached a five-year high in 2025, with the largest number of deaths recorded in Southeast Asia, largely driven by Myanmar’s civil war.
A report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines found civilians were the most affected, making up some 84 percent of the 6,929 casualties recorded in 2025, half of them were children.
In Myanmar, where both the government and armed groups are using landmines, 1,891 deaths were recorded in 2025, the highest number of any country for the third consecutive year.
On average, five people are killed or wounded by landmines daily in Myanmar, the report found.
“Myanmar has gone beyond crisis to catastrophe, and has claimed the ignoble title of top producer of landmine victims for a third year in a row,” said Yeshua Moser-Puangsuwan, a co-author of the Landmine Monitor 2026 report.
“There is now contamination at some level in almost two-thirds of the townships of the country.”
Myanmar – along with Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and other countries in the region – accounted for 27 percent of global deaths from landmines in 2025, despite having only 8 percent of the world’s population.
Syria saw a spike of more than 50 percent in casualties, with 1,602 deaths recorded in 2025 after large numbers of civilians returned after the fall of ousted President Bashar al-Assad in 2024.
“Syria is huge, but it is a post-war crisis,” Moser-Puangsuwan said. “People are now returning, and that is driving the casualty figure. They need to radically scale up their clearance capacity.”
Five European countries opted out of Mine Ban Treaty
The International Campaign to Ban Landmines has been urging more countries to join the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty to end stockpiling, production and the transfer of antipersonnel mines.
Despite this, five countries on the borders with Russia – Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland – pulled out of the treaty, citing the “security situation in our region”.
Ukraine, meanwhile, notified the United Nations that it had decided to suspend the implementation of the treaty, even though such a move is not allowed under its provisions.
Russia, not a party to the treaty, has been making widespread use of mines in its invasion of Ukraine, and Landmine Monitor found that Ukraine had been using them as well.
Lebanon, the Marshall Islands and Tonga all joined the Mine Ban Treaty during the reporting period, and 162 countries are now bound by it.

items.title: Armed men take 25 hostages at supermarket in one of Colombia’s top tourist destinations
items.summary:
A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding 25 people hostage, the president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said on Tuesday.
De la Espriella, said the men were “common criminals” who fled into the supermarket after a fa
items.text:
A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding 25 people hostage, the president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said on Tuesday.
De la Espriella, said the men were “common criminals” who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
Military and police forces have been deployed to the hostage site, Colombian police said.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have shown footage of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
“Thirty people were kidnapped, five of whom have already been released. They are older women,” said de la Espriella from the city of Villavicencio, where he traveled after an overnight bombing there.
Cartagena is one of Colombia’s main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
The Rafael Núñez airport in Cartagena temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday after the incident, as the armed forces used one of the runways in connection with the incident. It later said operations were slowly returning to normal and landings were reopened about 45 minutes after the suspension.
Local media reported the hostages are being her at the Castellana location of the Éxito supermarket chain.

items.text:
Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.
Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.
The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.
The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.
Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

items.title: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
items.summary: Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-ful
items.text:
Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.
David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.
Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”
Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.
It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.
Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.
At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.
Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.
Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

items.title: UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
items.summary:
The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.
The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) s
items.text:
The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.
The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post.
The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.
The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.
While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.
“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.
The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.
The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”
The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

items.title: Experts Raise Alarm Over Lenient Penalties in Proposed Pesticide Bill
items.summary: NAKURU, Kenya Nov 24 – Organic farming lobby groups and environmental and agricultural experts have raised concerns over proposed penalties for pesticide-related offences, warning that the fines and prison terms outlined in the Pest Control Products Bill, 2025, may not be strong enough to deter offe
items.text:
NAKURU, Kenya Nov 24 – Organic farming lobby groups and environmental and agricultural experts have raised concerns over proposed penalties for pesticide-related offences, warning that the fines and prison terms outlined in the Pest Control Products Bill, 2025, may not be strong enough to deter offenders.
The stakeholders argue that the proposed fines are disproportionately low compared to the profits made from importing and selling hazardous, banned and counterfeit pesticides, raising questions about the effectiveness of the legislation in protecting public health and the environment.
The Bill, which is awaiting the Committee of the Whole House stage in the National Assembly, proposes fines of up to Sh50,000 or imprisonment for six months, or both, for providing false information during product registration.
Similar penalties apply to unauthorised research and certain violations involving pesticide transportation.
The highest penalty for importing, selling or using unregistered pest control products is a fine of Sh1 million or imprisonment for two years, or both.
However, counterfeit pesticide-related offences attract significantly higher penalties, with proposed fines ranging from Sh2 million to Sh10 million, imprisonment for up to seven years, or both.
Speaking during a media roundtable organised by Media for Science, Health and Agriculture (MESHA), Growth Partners Africa Director Dr Daniel Maingi questioned whether the proposed punishments would sufficiently discourage violations.
Maingi said the Bill lacked adequate provisions to ensure manufacturers and distributors take responsibility for the environmental consequences of their products.
He called for the incorporation of the polluter-pays principle through mechanisms such as Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR).
“EPR makes manufacturers and brand owners responsible for managing the environmental impact of their products throughout their lifecycle,” he said.
Maingi further noted that the proposed legislation did not explicitly provide for criminal liability for manufacturers or distributors in cases where pesticide use resulted in environmental contamination or poisoning.

Colombia at a Crossroads: Searching for peace amid conflict
A decade after Colombia’s peace accords, former FARC fighter and artist honours killed signatories with a mural.
Yuheni Izquierdo, a former FARC fighter turned artist, paints a mural commemorating fellow peace signatories killed since Colombia’s 2016 Havana peace accords. More than 50 years of armed conflict formally ended with the agreement, but hundreds of signatories have since been killed as armed groups carry out reprisals and fight for territorial control.
Yuheni fears that the escalating violence threatens to return the country to a past that claimed more than 450,000 lives and hopes her mural will inspire Colombians to believe that a lasting peace is possible.
Colombia at a Crossroads is a documentary film by Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi.

items.title: Kenya’s coding and green skills give its youth a head start as Africa readies the world’s largest workforce – report
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – Kenya’s push to teach coding and green skills in secondary school puts its young people ahead of much of Africa as the continent prepares the largest generation of workers the world has seen, a new report says.
The Mastercard Foundation report, Secondary Education in Africa:
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – Kenya’s push to teach coding and green skills in secondary school puts its young people ahead of much of Africa as the continent prepares the largest generation of workers the world has seen, a new report says.
The Mastercard Foundation report, Secondary Education in Africa: Expanding Pathways to Work, Livelihoods, and Lifelong Learning, was launched in Accra, Ghana, on Tuesday at a gathering attended by the ministers of education of Ghana, Liberia, Rwanda and Sierra Leone.
By 2035, more than 330 million young people in Sub-Saharan Africa will reach working age, more than in the rest of the world combined. Only 9 per cent go on to university or college, making secondary school the last stage of formal education for most.
Mastercard Foundation President and CEO Sewit Ahderom said secondary school is “where we can make the biggest difference to whether they find dignified and fulfilling work.”
Kenya’s digital and green edge
The report highlights Kenya, with Rwanda, for teaching computer programming in secondary school, and names it with Nigeria and Zambia as offering some coverage of artificial intelligence topics, at a time when a scan of 49 Sub-Saharan countries found only two that explicitly build AI into their curricula.
Kenyan youth are already earning online. A study cited in the report, covering Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa and Uganda, found that selling online, from airtime and data bundles to mobile money services and retail goods, was the most common form of gig work for young people. The report also points to Kobo360, an e-logistics platform that helps truck drivers in Kenya and four other countries find work and access finance.
On green jobs, the report says Kenya “has one of the most advanced approaches to teaching cross-cutting green skills,” with short courses in renewable energy, environmental management and sustainable construction, and the KenGen Geothermal Training Centre serving as a regional centre of excellence.
What school is for
The report finds the world of work is changing fast. More than 10 million young Africans enter the labour market each year, but only about three million formal jobs are created, and around 90 per cent of youth employment is informal. It calls on schools to prepare young people for wage jobs, self-employment and entrepreneurship, as well as digital, green, care and creative work.
“When we published the first Secondary Education in Africa report in 2020, we set out to show that secondary education is the main pathway to work for young people in Africa. Six years on, that message is more important than ever. This second report builds on what we have learned together and asks a bigger question: not only how many young people are in school, but what school prepares them for,” said Samuel Yalew Adela, Senior Director, Secondary Education and Transitions at the Mastercard Foundation.
The creative economy is one of the bright spots. Africa’s music industry is the fastest growing in the world, the report notes, and film, digital media, fashion and gaming offer growing openings for young people.
Every learner counts
The report says reaching the learners most often left behind is good economics as well as fair. Sierra Leone, one of seven countries studied in depth, has made fee-free schooling and the inclusion of pregnant girls, learners with disabilities and rural learners national policy.
“In Sierra Leone, radical inclusion means that no young person is left out because of poverty, pregnancy, disability, or where they live. Fee-free schooling has brought more young people into our classrooms. The evidence in this report shows that reaching the last learner is not only a matter of justice; it is how we build the workforce our economy needs,” said Hon. Conrad Sackey, Sierra Leone’s Minister of Basic and Senior Secondary Education.
Kenya has a similar goal in its 100 per cent transition policy, which saw 97 per cent of learners who completed Grade 6 in 2025 move on to junior school.
“The Mastercard Foundation is committed to working alongside governments and partners to turn this evidence into action, so that young people leave school able to earn a living and build a future on their own terms,” Ahderom said.

items.title: Senegal reinstated as Africa Cup of Nations winners over Morocco by CAS ruling
items.summary:
More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal are Africa's champions once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.
Senegal won the A
items.text:
More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal are Africa's champions once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.
Senegal won the Africa Cup of Nations on the field in a chaotic final in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because their players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
- AFCON 2025 Final: Nothing could have been more embarrassing for African football
CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, citing referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.
"Once again and forever, champions of Africa," the Senegalese soccer federation posted on social media.
Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."
Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game, CAS added.
"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."
The Moroccan federation (FRMF) released a statement confirming its intention to "pursue all available legal avenues" to appeal against the decision.
The federation alleged there had been "communication" between a member of the CAS panel and the president of the Senegalese federation 48 hours before the decision was issued.
The FRMF said these practices would "compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration procedure."
The FRMF added that the decision "did not take into account the approach recently adopted by both the International Football Association Board (IFAB) and FIFA, regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee's permission, and the resulting disciplinary responsibilities and penalties."
CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court though only on limited procedural grounds.
Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.
The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).
Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.
Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Brahim Diaz was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.
The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point. Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.
Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.
The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met -- both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.
In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."
The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.
The Senegalese federation (FSF) said it welcomed the ruling with "deep satisfaction."
"Far from consecrating the pre-eminence of one party over another, this decision affirms above all the triumph of sporting fairness and recalls a cardinal principle: the truth of a match is established exclusively on the field, under the protection of sports law," the federation said in its statement.
The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.
Th Associated Press and PA contributed to this report.

items.title: Man United win appeal over Yoro red card against Liverpool
items.summary:
Manchester United have won their appeal over Leny Yoro's red card against Liverpool.
The Frenchman was dismissed after eight minutes at Anfield after a challenge on Alexander Isak. On-field referee Sam Barrott decided Yoro had denied a clear goalscoring opportunity, a view backed up by VAR John Broo
items.text:
Manchester United have won their appeal over Leny Yoro's red card against Liverpool.
The Frenchman was dismissed after eight minutes at Anfield after a challenge on Alexander Isak. On-field referee Sam Barrott decided Yoro had denied a clear goalscoring opportunity, a view backed up by VAR John Brooks.
United, who lost 4-0 in Mauricio Pochettino's first game as head coach, launched an appeal on Monday, insisting that Isak's heavy touch meant he would not have had the chance to score.
The Football Association announced on Tuesday that the claim of wrongful dismissal has been upheld and Yoro's one-match ban has been lifted.
A statement issued by the FA read: "Leny Yoro's one-match suspension has been removed following a successful claim of wrongful dismissal.
"The Manchester United player was sent off for denying an obvious goal scoring opportunity during their Premier League match against Liverpool on Sunday Nov. 22."
Bruno Fernandes: Leny Yoro foul 'never a red card'
Bruno Fernandes told the BBC that it was "never a red card," adding: "I think it's too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR, seated, with such a long time to see and put it back, go forward, put it back, do it in slow motion, whatsoever.
"To make a mistake like this can change a game. But obviously, then, it's not because of them that we concede the goal from the free-kick, but it changes completely the flow of the game."
Pochettino said: "I wasn't agreeing with the red card because I think the situation was when Isak control the ball, the ball wasn't in his control."
Kobbie Mainoo added: "The ball is already with the keeper when he's gone down, two players running at full speed. I mean, it's impossible to be a red, but it is what it is."
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola defended the referee's decision, saying: "[Yoro] is clearly the last man, it is clearly a foul. Would Alex or the 'keeper arrive first to the ball? We will never know. It's a clear foul, he's a last player, Alex goes against the 'keeper."
It's the second major refereeing error in a game involving United this season. In September, referee's body Pro Ref apologised after Erling Haaland's goal at Old Trafford was mistakenly allowed to stand.
City, who were reduced to 10 men in the first half after Phil Foden's red card, won the game 1-0.

items.title: Bayern hold 'constructive' talks with Musiala's agents over health, not money
items.summary:
MUNICH -- Jamal Musiala's health, rather than his wages, were up for discussion as Bayern Munich officials met with the star player's agents Tuesday, the club's board member for sport Max Eberl said.
The meeting comes days after Bayern was criticized by global players' union FIFPRO for what it calle
items.text:
MUNICH -- Jamal Musiala's health, rather than his wages, were up for discussion as Bayern Munich officials met with the star player's agents Tuesday, the club's board member for sport Max Eberl said.
The meeting comes days after Bayern was criticized by global players' union FIFPRO for what it called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala" after he suffered seizures, and right before Bayern flew out for Wednesday's Champions League game against Lille in France.
Describing the talks as "very, very constructive," Eberl said the focus was on Musiala's recovery from a recent injury, in remarks reported by the dpa news agency.
"Today it was about just how we want to get Jamal back on the field, just like before his muscle injury in the international break," Eberl said. "That's the only task FC Bayern has currently, to give Jamal this trust and not some topics about money or something."
Some prominent figures at Bayern had questioned whether Musiala can recover his previous form, and suggested that his contract extension signed last year may no longer reflect the player he has become.
The suggestion that a contract could be renegotiated because of poor health drew unusually sharp criticism from FIFPRO.
"Contracts are there to be respected," the players' union said Saturday. "An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."
Musiala has rarely played since collapsing during preseason games in August, and has also had a muscle injury. He was among Bayern's squad of 20 players traveling to the Lille game Tuesday.
Musiala previously posted on social media that he was diagnosed with "absence seizures caused by a neurological dysfunction," that it wasn't a risk to his health, and he intended to keep playing.
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany, who has had his own health issues this season, has backed Musiala publicly and said in September it wouldn't be "a big deal" if the seizures return.

items.title: Flick on Barcelona with no Yamal: 'We can win without him'
items.summary:
Barcelona head coach Hansi Flick has said the Spanish champions know how to cope without Lamine Yamal with the teenager set to miss Wednesday's Champions League game against Sabah in Azerbaijan.
Yamal, 19, has not travelled with his teammates to Baku due to an ankle problem, but should be back for B
items.text:
Barcelona head coach Hansi Flick has said the Spanish champions know how to cope without Lamine Yamal with the teenager set to miss Wednesday's Champions League game against Sabah in Azerbaijan.
Yamal, 19, has not travelled with his teammates to Baku due to an ankle problem, but should be back for Barça's LaLiga game at Deportivo A Coruña on Sunday.
It will be the first time this season Barça have played without Yamal, who has started all 17 of their matches until now, scoring 13 goals and providing 13 assists.
"We have played without Lamine in the past, we know what to do," Flick said in the pre-game news conference on Tuesday.
"He is very important for us, but [on Monday] we checked and decided it is better he stays at home. Hopefully, everything works well and he's available for the weekend."
Karim Adeyemi and Gabriel Jesus are among the options to replace Yamal against Sabah alongside Anthony Gordon and Raphinha in attack, although Flick said he has not decided what the team will be yet.
"A player like Lamine will always be missed," midfielder Frenkie de Jong, speaking before Flick, said.
"He is a player with extraordinary talent. He creates danger and chances on his own, so you notice when a player like him is not there. But the squad is full of good players and we can win without him."
De Jong may have to continue out of position at centre-back as Barça remain without Andreas Christensen and Xavi Espart in defence, while Flick suggested Pau Cubarsí may not be risked as he recovers from a hip injury.
"The thing I like most about Frenkie is that he said 'OK, coach, if you need me as a centre-back or a full-back, it doesn't matter,'" Flick explained.
"He said he's available and he can help the team. This is, for me, a team player. He gives everything for this team.
"We all know he is one of the best midfielders in the world. I see him as a midfielder, we need his quality there, but at the moment we will see where we need him tomorrow."
De Jong, who has made five appearances this season since returning from a knee injury, also stressed that he sees himself as a midfielder long-term.
"I consider myself a midfielder, everyone knows that," De Jong said. "I have always played there. But if team needs me elsewhere or the coach considers it better I play in another position, I will always do it."
Barça, who lead LaLiga with 12 wins from 13 games, have made an encouraging start in the Champions League, winning three of their four games.
Their one loss came against back-to-back winners Paris Saint-Germain, but De Jong feels the Catalan side can compete with the French champions to win a first European trophy since 2015.
"The demand at Barça is always to win it," he said. "That is the objective, but that doesn't mean it would be a failure or a bad season if we don't.
"There are at least six other teams with the same objective, but we believe we can compete and are capable of winning it.
"For now, PSG are favourites, they won it in each of the last two years and they beat us this season. So, we have to improve and demonstrate at the end of the season that we are better."
De Jong: Every Sabah player will be '100% motivated'
Sabah, meanwhile, have won just one of their four matches in their debut campaign in the Champions League.
However, with the 4,000-kilometre flight representing Barça's longest every journey for a domestic game, Flick is not underestimating the challenge.
"Sabah are a team who love to play football," he said. "They have clear patterns and are brave to play out. For me, the most important thing is to play with the right attitude.
"They are for the first time in their history in the Champions League, they love to play against teams like Barcelona and Manchester United, it's special. Every player will be 100% motivated; we need the same mentality from our players."

items.title: Fiona the hippo to be honored by FC Cincinnati with tifo after untimely death
items.summary:
FC Cincinnati will honor Fiona, the local hippo who became famous on social media, following her unexpected death last week.
The MLS side is planning to unveil a special tifo to pay tribute to Fiona prior to their MLS Cup playoff match against Nashville on Saturday.
Fiona was beloved by many in Cinc
items.text:
FC Cincinnati will honor Fiona, the local hippo who became famous on social media, following her unexpected death last week.
The MLS side is planning to unveil a special tifo to pay tribute to Fiona prior to their MLS Cup playoff match against Nashville on Saturday.
Fiona was beloved by many in Cincinnati, Ohio, and around the world. Fiona died of health complications last Thursday following after she swallowed a child's knit cap that had landed in her enclosure at Cincinnati Zoo.
The Nile hippopotamus became a worldwide sensation when she was born in 2017 at the zoo. Fiona arrived six weeks premature and her chances of survival were low.
But she beat the odds to make it through and grew into a viral star.
In 2017, local ice cream chain Graeter's even released a limited-edition flavor inspired by Fiona. It was called "Chunky Chunky Hippo."
FC Cincinnati said Fiona "became a symbol of Cincinnati and captured hearts around the world."
During FC Cincinnati's 3-1 win over Orlando on the day of Fiona's death, defender Nick Hagglund dedicated his goal to the hippo by exclaiming "that's for Fiona" before mimicking her ears on the top of his head.
Fiona was also honored by other Cincinnati sports teams upon news of her death, including NFL team Cincinnati Bengals and MLB side Cincinnati Reds. They both posted tributes to the much-loved hippo on their social media accounts.
- Bengals, Reds pay tribute to Fiona the hippo after her death
- NFL Week 11 arrivals: Tee Higgins pays homage to Fiona the Hippo ahead of 'MNF'
Bengals wide receiver Tee Higgins even wore a Fiona sweater on Monday night before his team lost to the Washington Commanders.
FC Cincinnati will also make a donation for every fan in attendance at TQL Stadium to the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden in Fiona's memory.
Speaking about Fiona's death, the Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said: "Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore.
"She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many."
FC Cincinnati can progress to the Eastern Conference semifinal with a win over Nashville on Saturday.

items.title: United States to host Copa América for 2nd straight edition in 2028
items.summary:
The Copa América will be returning to the United States for the second straight edition in 2028, the governing bodies of South America (CONMEBOL) and North, Central America and the Caribbean (Concacaf) confirmed Tuesday.
The U.S. previously hosted South America's quadrennial championship in 2024, as
items.text:
The Copa América will be returning to the United States for the second straight edition in 2028, the governing bodies of South America (CONMEBOL) and North, Central America and the Caribbean (Concacaf) confirmed Tuesday.
The U.S. previously hosted South America's quadrennial championship in 2024, as well as special centenary edition in 2016. The 2028 edition will take place from June 9 to July 9, finishing before the start of the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles on July 14.
The host cities are yet to be confirmed.
"The CONMEBOL Copa América is much more than a tournament: it is part of our identity, our history, and the greatness of South American football," CONMEBOL president and FIFA vice president Alejandro Domínguez said in a joint statement.
"In 2028, we will once again bring that passion to the United States, reaffirming our historic partnership with Concacaf and our shared commitment to continuing to drive the growth of football across the continent. This new edition will be another opportunity to demonstrate that football knows no borders and that, when we Believe Big, we can go even further."
As in 2024, the tournament will feature all 10 South American teams -- including record five-time World Cup winner Brazil and finalists at the last three World Cups, Argentina -- as well as six from Concacaf.
The six participating Concacaf teams will be determined by the results of the 2027 Gold Cup.
"This agreement will bring six Concacaf national teams a new opportunity to compete against some of the best in the world, while further reinforcing the competitive significance of our Concacaf Gold Cup," Concacaf president and FIFA vice president Victor Montagliani said.
"We look forward to working alongside CONMEBOL, the host venues, and other key parties to organize a first-class tournament that reflects the passion, quality and potential of football across the continent."
The 2024 edition saw Argentina defeat Colombia in a final that was marred by an 82-minute delay following a security breach in which fans broke through one of the main entry gates at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, Florida.
A settlement was reached last year in a class action lawsuit that was filed by fans in the wake of the chaotic scenes, with some fans with tickets unable to enter the venue, while others left early out of concern for their safety.
The USMNT was eliminated in the group stage of the 2024 Copa América under Gregg Berhalter after defeats to Uruguay and Panama. That paved the way for Mauricio Pochettino's arrival as coach, and he led the USMNT as co-hosts of the 2026 World Cup to the round of 16. Pochettino left for Manchester United this month.
U.S. Soccer is currently seeking a permanent replacement as head coach.
Argentina has won the Copa América a record 16 times, including the last two editions when it was led by star Lionel Messi. However, the Inter Miami forward will not be a part of the 2028 edition after retiring from international duty last month.

items.title: Pope Francis’ private diary reveals 3 encounters with the devil
items.summary:
MOMBASA, Kenya, Nov 24 — Pope Francis recalled seeing the devil in the choir area during Mass in a personal diary spanning more than three decades, one of two occasions on which the late pontiff said he saw the figure, according to excerpts published by the Vatican on Tuesday.
The revelations are co
items.text:
MOMBASA, Kenya, Nov 24 — Pope Francis recalled seeing the devil in the choir area during Mass in a personal diary spanning more than three decades, one of two occasions on which the late pontiff said he saw the figure, according to excerpts published by the Vatican on Tuesday.
The revelations are contained in The Personal Diary of Pope Francis, a 160-page collection of writings covering the period between 1992 and 2024.
The entries offer an unusually intimate account of the late pontiff’s spiritual life, including his fears, moments of vulnerability and struggles during his 12-year papacy.
In one entry, Francis recalled seeing the devil from a car and, on another occasion, in the choir area during Mass.
He described the figure as having menacing eyes and wrote of feeling that it was lying in wait for him.
The diary also records another encounter in which Francis heard the devil’s voice, alongside a prolonged period of spiritual turmoil between 2021 and 2022, which he associated with illness and what he described as decisive assaults by the forces of evil.
“I clearly heard the voice of the devil,” he wrote.
In a 2016 reflection, he wrote: “If the devil is attacking so blatantly, it is because I do not have much time left and he wants his prey.”
Spiritual crisis
The entries reveal how Francis understood his struggles through the lens of Catholic spirituality, often interpreting difficult moments as a contest between good and evil.
The period coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic, which brought unprecedented disruption to daily life and left even the Vatican’s normally busy surroundings unusually deserted.
In March 2020, Francis delivered an extraordinary Urbi et Orbi (“to the City and to the World”) blessing in an almost empty St Peter’s Square, in one of the most striking images of his pontificate.
In his diary, the Pope described feeling vulnerable to temptation, including what he called “pagan seduction”, and recorded how prayer and devotion helped him resist.
Pope Francis frequently turned to the Rosary and the intercession of the Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus Christ, whom Catholics honour as the Blessed Virgin and ask to intercede on their behalf.
“The Virgin saved me,” he wrote.
His diary also reveals the personal anxieties that accompanied his leadership of the Catholic Church. At various points, he expressed fear that he was unequal to the responsibilities of the papacy or might cause harm to others.
“I am afraid,” he wrote in one entry, even asking God to take him away.
The writings also capture moments of consolation. Reflecting on his relationship with Jesus, Francis wrote of feeling the merciful gaze of Christ and recalled that “He smiled” at him.
Personal struggle to spiritual renewal
The period of spiritual difficulty appears to have informed some of Francis’ later reflections on faith, suffering and divine love.
Two documents published during the final years of his pontificate were particularly connected to themes reflected in the diary, Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández who put together the Pope’s writtings noted.
In 2023, he issued C’est la confiance, an apostolic exhortation marking the 150th anniversary of the birth of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, whose spirituality emphasised trust in God’s love and mercy.
The following year, he published Dilexit nos, an encyclical on the human and divine love of Jesus Christ, expressed through devotion to his Sacred Heart.
The diary also reveals his devotion to Saint Joseph and Our Lady of Fatima, whom he continued to invoke during moments of personal difficulty. In one 2023 entry, he recorded turning to the Virgin Mary in prayer.
How the diary came to be
The collection was edited by Cardinal Fernández, Prefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and a close associate of Francis.
Fernández recalled that the late Pope had shown him an old diary or planner at Casa Santa Marta, where Francis lived during his pontificate, and indicated that others would eventually decide what to do with the writings.
Following Francis’ death, Fernández sought the approval of his successor, Pope Leo XIV, before proceeding with publication.
The selection and preparation of the material took more than a year. The book is being released in five languages and distributed in 94 countries, with the English edition published by Penguin Random House in the United States and United Kingdom.
The publication offers a rare glimpse into the private reflections of a Pope, whose personal writings were not originally intended as a public account of his spiritual life.
The man behind the papacy
Born Jorge Mario Bergoglio in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on December 17, 1936, Francis was elected Pope on March 13, 2013, becoming the first pontiff from the Americas and the first Jesuit to lead the Catholic Church.
He chose the name Francis in honour of Saint Francis of Assisi, whose life was associated with simplicity, humility and concern for the poor.
During his 12-year pontificate, he repeatedly called for a Church that was more welcoming, attentive to people on the margins and engaged with the challenges facing the modern world.
His leadership was also marked by efforts to reform the Vatican administration, address clerical sexual abuse and encourage greater transparency and accountability within the Church.
Francis died on April 21, 2025, aged 88. He was succeeded by Leo XIV, who was elected on May 8, 2025.
Four encyclicals and a lasting legacy
Francis published four encyclicals during his pontificate, addressing faith, environmental protection, human fraternity and Christian spirituality.
His first, Lumen fidei (2013), explored the role of faith in Christian life. The document had been started by his predecessor, Pope Benedict XVI, and was completed by Francis.

items.text:

Jannik Sinner has successfully undergone surgery on his right knee; casting doubt over his Australian Open participation; You can watch the Next Gen ATP Finals from 9-13 December in Reggio Calabria, Italy live on Sky Sports Tennis
Tuesday 24 November 2026 17:50, UK
Former world No 1 Jannik Sinner has undergone surgery on his troublesome knee, casting doubt over his hopes of playing at the Australian Open.
The 25-year-old has not played since winning his fifth Grand Slam ‌title at Wimbledon in July.
The Italian world No 2 said this month he was confident of returning in time for the Australian Open, which starts on January 17, but would not rush his recovery.

Sky Italy are reporting he could be out for up to three months.
Five-time Grand Slam champion Sinner posted on social media: "Over the past few months, together with my team we've tried everything to treat my injury without surgery. After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn't respond as we'd all hoped, that's why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band.
"I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team. Thank you for all your support. See you soon."
Sinner was operated on in Turku, on the southwest coast of Finland, by renowned surgeon Lasse Lempainen.
The procedure involved lengthening the iliotibial band through arthroscopy, using small Z-shaped incisions to reduce tension in the area.
His knee will initially be immobilised before he begins intensive physiotherapy to regain mobility and strength, with his return to full fitness for 2027 unclear.
Sinner said he had lost a significant amount of weight after having his tonsils removed and was in the process of rebuilding muscle.
He recently parted ways with his Australian coach Darren Cahill, with Swede Magnus Norman joining his coaching setup.
Seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz, who won the ATP Finals title for the first time on Sunday, is the defending Australian Open champion.

items.title: European court: States can turn back migrants in some cases
items.summary:
European court: States can turn back migrants in some cases
November 24, 2026
The European Court of Human Rights on Tuesday ruled that states belonging to the Council of Europe group have a right to control foreign arrivals.
But the 46 member states of the group — that includes all EU and some non-E
items.text:
European court: States can turn back migrants in some cases
November 24, 2026
The European Court of Human Rights on Tuesday ruled that states belonging to the Council of Europe group have a right to control foreign arrivals.
But the 46 member states of the group — that includes all EU and some non-EU countries and promotes democracy and human rights on the continent — must ensure and uphold human rights of people even in hostile environments.
The European court ruling is a complicated one since it deals with a case concerning the entry of nationals of Afghanistan, Iraq and Cuba into EU member countries Poland, Latvia and Lithuania between 2021 and 2022.
That was a time when a border standoff was playing out between Belarus and the EU's eastern member states, with Belarus having been accused of entirely manufacturing a migration crisis to put pressure on the EU.
Belarus arranged for people from various third countries to enter their state and then pointed them to the EU's frontiers.
Europe's human rights court says countries can turn back migrants with duty of care
Europe's most important human rights court on Tuesday ruled that states have a right to control the entry of foreign nationals into their territory even when migration has been weaponized.
The court calls Belarus' hostile actions of 2021 as having been an instance of "instrumentalization of migration."
But the court said that states must still ensure that migrants are protected against inhumane or degrading treatment.
In the context of a surge in migration, for example, national authorities were still to identify people who were particularly at risk of suffering or enduring ill treatment.
The migrants in the case brought before the European court said that they had been violently prevented from crossing into the EU without their asylum applications having been examined and that their human rights had been violated.
"In a context of instrumentalization of migration, the removal of a foreign national to the instrumentalizing state would not, as such, constitute a violation of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman and degrading treatment)," the court press release said.
The court ordered Poland, Latvia and Lithuania to pay compensation for their treatment of migrants at the EU's external borders with Belarus.
Five EU countries announce plan with Rwanda to establish 'return hub'
Five EU countries also last week announced a plan with Rwanda to establish a so-called return hub in the African nation.
The hub will host rejected asylum seekers waiting to return to their countries of origin.
But there are many concerns about the project since Rwanda ranks low on human rights measures and there are questions about whether people's rights will be sufficiently protected.

items.title: Cameroon separatist leader pleads not guilty at war crimes trial in Norway
items.summary:
Cameroon separatist leader pleads not guilty at war crimes trial in Norway
Lucas Cho Ayaba is accused of remotely planning attacks that killed and injured dozens of civilians.
Cameroonian separatist leader Lucas Cho Ayaba has pleaded not guilty in a Norwegian court to being an accessory to war crime
items.text:
Cameroon separatist leader pleads not guilty at war crimes trial in Norway
Lucas Cho Ayaba is accused of remotely planning attacks that killed and injured dozens of civilians.
Cameroonian separatist leader Lucas Cho Ayaba has pleaded not guilty in a Norwegian court to being an accessory to war crimes and “terrorism”, charges that carry a sentence of up to 30 years.
The 54-year-old, who appeared in a court in Oslo on Tuesday, is accused of involvement in planning two attacks in Cameroon from Norway, helping to select targets and pay for explosives.
Prosecutors say Ayaba, also known as Cho Lucas Yabah, remotely led the separatist Amazonia Governing Council and commanded its armed wing, the Amazonia Defence Forces, from 2017 until 2024, when he was arrested in Norway, where he has lived since 2008.
Francophone-majority Cameroon has been gripped for nearly 10 years by conflict between state security forces and separatists demanding the independence of two Anglophone regions in the country’s west to form what supporters call “Ambazonia”.
In February 2023, three improvised devices exploded during a mountain run race near Buea in southwestern Cameroon, killing a 38-year-old woman and injuring 19 civilians.
In February of the following year, another improvised device killed a 15-year-old girl during a Youth Day celebration in Nkambe, northwestern Cameroon. More than 90 civilians were wounded, with some undergoing amputations.
‘Send him to hell’
Ayaba is also alleged to have encouraged or ordered the murder or attempted murder of captives and to have orchestrated the torture or humiliation of four women accused of having intimate relations with Cameroonian soldiers.
“Messages on WhatsApp are key evidence in this case,” prosecutor Carl Fredrik Fari told the AFP news agency.
“Wrap a rope around his neck and send him to hell,” Ayaba allegedly said in an audio message sent on WhatsApp in October 2023, after receiving videos showing a mistreated prisoner believed to be a Cameroonian soldier.
Ayaba’s lawyer, Morten Engesbak, told AFP that Ayaba “sees himself as the leader of a struggle to liberate a population that has been oppressed for very many years by the Cameroonian authorities”.
The unrest began in late 2016 after Anglophone lawyers and teachers protested against the appointment of Francophone magistrates unfamiliar with British common law to courts in English-speaking regions, and French-speaking teachers unable to communicate fluently in English.
The protests were met with a violent government crackdown and eventually gave rise to a separatist movement seeking independence for the two regions.
The UN says at least 6,000 civilians have been killed since 2016. More than 330,000 people were displaced within Cameroon in 2026 and another 100,000 took refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.
The trial in the Oslo district court is expected to last until March 12.

items.title: Murkomen Orders Crackdown on Illegal Firearms After Isiolo-Garissa Clashes
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has directed the Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja to roll out an intensive, intelligence-led operation to recover illegal firearms in Isiolo and Garissa counties following deadly inter-communal violence along the border.
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has directed the Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja to roll out an intensive, intelligence-led operation to recover illegal firearms in Isiolo and Garissa counties following deadly inter-communal violence along the border.
Murkomen said the operation would target illegal weapons believed to be contributing to insecurity in the region, which has recently experienced renewed tensions resulting in loss of lives and destruction of property.
In a statement following a consultative meeting with leaders from the two counties on Tuesday, Murkomen said the government was committed to restoring peace and normalcy in the affected areas.
He said the meeting assessed the security situation, examined the underlying causes of the conflict and identified gaps requiring urgent intervention.
Among the resolutions was a comprehensive assessment of security deployment in the two counties, with the National Police Service expected to reposition security installations and increase police presence in affected areas.
The Inspector General was also tasked with assessing the mobility needs of security personnel and prioritising the region in the forthcoming allocation of police vehicles.
Murkomen further directed the National Police Service to review the National Police Reservists (NPR) in the two counties through vetting and retraining, while replacing officers found to be misusing their firearms.
The government also resolved to strengthen and provide resources to peace committees while establishing a framework for sharing natural resources among communities living along the border.
Other interventions include improving mobile network coverage through engagements with telecommunications companies and fast-tracking funding for the construction of security roads in the affected areas.
Murkomen said a security team led by him would visit the region to assess the implementation of the agreed interventions, alongside immediate peace meetings involving local communities.
He condemned the killings and conveyed condolences to families who lost their loved ones, urging residents and political leaders to promote peaceful coexistence.

Gunmen hold two dozen people hostage at supermarket in Colombia's Cartagena
Armed robbers took roughly two dozen people hostage at a supermarket in Colombia’s tourist city of Cartagena on Tuesday, prompting a major police operation and the temporary suspension of incoming flights, authorities said.
items.text:
Gunmen hold two dozen people hostage at supermarket in Colombia's Cartagena
Armed robbers took roughly two dozen people hostage at a supermarket in Colombia’s tourist city of Cartagena on Tuesday, prompting a major police operation and the temporary suspension of incoming flights, authorities said. Landings at Rafael Nunez airport resumed about 45 minutes later, after the military used a runway during the operation.
Twenty-five people are being held hostage at a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena, President Abelardo De La Espriella said on Tuesday, adding ‌that military and police forces have been deployed.
Five older women who were being held ‌have already been released, he said.
Reuters images showed heavily armed military and police gathered outside the supermarket.
"Thirty people were kidnapped, five of whom have already been released. They are ‌older women," said De La Espriella from the city of Villavicencio, where he traveled following an overnight ‌bombing there.
"All the capabilities of our various security forces, have now been deployed, including special units," he added.
Read moreA president among body bags: Photo ops spark outrage in Colombia
The Rafael Nunez airport in Cartagena briefly suspended landings as the armed forces used one of the runways in connection with the incident. Landings were reopened about 45 minutes after the suspension.
Local media reported the hostages are being at the Castellana location of the Exito supermarket chain.
Images on social media showed some people kneeling against the windows of the store earlier on Tuesday, their hands seemingly bound. Reuters could not immediately independently verify the images.

items.title: US sanctions on Lebanon’s Hezbollah-affiliates may have limited impact
items.summary:
US sanctions on Lebanon’s Hezbollah-affiliates may have limited impact
Analysts say US sanctions unlikely to weaken Hezbollah significantly, but risk hurting the Lebanese populace.
Beirut, Lebanon – New United States sanctions on an organisation linked to the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah
items.text:
US sanctions on Lebanon’s Hezbollah-affiliates may have limited impact
Analysts say US sanctions unlikely to weaken Hezbollah significantly, but risk hurting the Lebanese populace.
Beirut, Lebanon – New United States sanctions on an organisation linked to the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah will have a limited impact beyond the political messaging the punishment provides, analysts have told Al Jazeera.
The organisation – a charity called Wa Ta’awanu Association – was among the entities and individuals targeted by the US Treasury in new sanctions announced on November 18, accusing it of being a “front organisation” for Hezbollah. The Treasury said the sanctions were an effort to disrupt Hezbollah’s financing networks.
The sanctions are part of a US campaign against Hezbollah, a Shia political and military group. Washington has put pressure on the Lebanese government to make progress on disarming Hezbollah, which has been engaged in an on-off war with Israel for the past 40 years.
But experts told Al Jazeera, the sanctions will do little to change Lebanon’s domestic situation, in which Hezbollah has been one of the major powers – if not the major power – over the past two decades.
“[The US] is threatening to impose sanctions on political, judicial and security figures but that won’t change the reality,” Qassem Kassir, a Lebanese journalist close to Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera. “Sanctions or the threat of sanctions will not change the reality inside Lebanon.”
Lebanese media reports have suggested that the US, frustrated by the Lebanese government’s lack of progress in disarming the Iran-backed group, could apply sanctions beyond direct Hezbollah affiliates and start to target bankers and businessmen.
“There are other packages, a second, third, maybe a fourth [round of sanctions],” Ali Hamade, a Lebanese journalist with Annahar, claimed in a video posted to social media. “It will focus on Hezbollah funding and money smuggling efforts and may involve several bankers, figures in the world of Lebanese finance and business, in the real estate sector and contractors.
He added that politicians, security personnel, judges, and figures in Lebanese public administration were unlikely to face sanctions yet.
Targeting Hezbollah-affiliated organisations
Hezbollah, a Shia-dominated movement which emerged during the Lebanese civil war, is part of a wider network of Iran-linked groups in the region. The group is believed to receive direct financing from Tehran, as well as its own financing networks.
In its sanctions announcement, the US Treasury claimed that the Wa Ta’awanu Association “provides cover for Hizballah’s activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services”.
But Kassir said the group provided assistance to needy Lebanese people.
“Unfortunately, the Americans and some Lebanese parties want to prevent any assistance or service from reaching people,” he said. “However, sanctions will not stop the work of the Wa Ta’awanu Association, just as it has not been able to stop the Al Qard Al Hassan, educational institutions, construction companies and Jihad Al-Binaa.”
Al Qard Al Hassan, a financial institution, and Jihad Al-Binaa, a construction company, are part of a wide array of Hezbollah-affiliated organisations that have been sanctioned by the US, though both companies also employ or serve people not affiliated with Hezbollah.
Sanctions as leverage
Israel has continued to attack what it says are Hezbollah targets in Lebanon intermittently, despite a “ceasefire” agreement earlier this year.
It also continues to hold territory it invaded up to 10km (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory.
Israel – backed by the US – has tied its withdrawal from Lebanon to the full disarmament of Hezbollah. Talks between the Israeli and Lebanese governments were held earlier this year and led to a Framework Agreement in June, which designated so-called “pilot zones” where Israeli troops would withdraw, and the Lebanese army would deploy to disarm Hezbollah.
But the pilot zone programme has had little success, as Israel still refuses to withdraw from new territories and accuses the Lebanese army of failing to disarm Hezbollah in the existing pilot zones.
In the meantime, the US has looked for other means to pressure Hezbollah, as it continues attacks against the group’s patron, Iran.
“The US treats sanctions as one of several forms of pressure that it can exert on Hezbollah’s financial networks,” David Wood, the senior Lebanon analyst with International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Washington has also targeted Hezbollah’s efforts to raise money outside of traditional financial systems – such as receiving physical cash – by insisting that the Lebanese state exert more control over the country’s airport, seaports and border with neighbouring Syria.”
But Wood argued that sanctions against the group and individuals connected to it are only likely to have a limited effect.
“The threat of US sanctions might change the behaviour of some Lebanese elites, but that source of leverage largely disappears after imposing sanctions, because it is not straightforward to lift them,” Wood said. “Imposing US sanctions seeks to raise the cost of doing business with Hezbollah, especially for alleged associates of the party who enjoy lucrative sources of private income. This tactic is probably less effective in relation to direct affiliates of Hezbollah, which are more likely to operate outside traditional financial networks already.”
A political tool
Analysts also argue that the US’s use of sanctions is politically driven, showing that it is not a neutral or balanced actor when it comes to brokering deals between Beirut and Tel Aviv.

Wirtz, 23, scored in Liverpool's 4-0 win over Manchester United on Sunday and has three goals and six
items.text:
Klopp advice and Iraola confidence boosts Wirtz
- Published
Florian Wirtz says he is enjoying his best form yet at Liverpool and benefiting from Andoni Iraola's confidence and Jurgen Klopp's advice.
Wirtz, 23, scored in Liverpool's 4-0 win over Manchester United on Sunday and has three goals and six assists this season.
The Germany midfielder made the £116m move from Bayer Leverkusen in the summer of 2025 and after failing to make his mark in his first campaign in England, is beginning to showcase his quality for Iraola's side.
Speaking in Belgium before Liverpool's Champions League game against Club Brugge, Wirtz said: "I can't really say that I've changed that much.
"I've become a bit better on a physical level and that's the only reason that could explain it."
He also said he has been picking the brains of Germany manager Klopp, the former Liverpool boss, while on international duty.
"He tells me all the time that he loved his time here, the people love him here and tries to give me some advice to get successful over here as he has shown how it is done," Wirtz said.
"He can give me some good advice. It's always small things. More private things.
"But he is speaking good about the club, the region, the people, and that helps to hear someone who has experienced it for a long time."
On the influence of Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot as Liverpool head coach in the summer, Wirtz added: "He is bringing me back in a place where I was maybe two years ago where I played really good football, and I can feel that he gives me the confidence and I'm really happy about that.
"I'm just trying to give him back what he gives me."
Liverpool have nine points from their four Champions League games, having won their first three before losing to Fenerbahce in Istanbul this month.
Cody Gakpo and Ryan Gravenberch are both absent from the travelling squad with injuries, with Iraola confirming that Gakpo will be out for the Merseyside derby this weekend, while adding that it is "difficult to say" for Gravenberch.

items.title: Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
items.summary:
Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen.
Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next
items.text:
Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen.
Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
The music streaming platform estimates that it will delete 29 million songs as a result of the AI ban.
The move comes just months after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing tracks identified as 100 percent AI-generated. In a post on X, Andersen says Tidal needed to take a more “drastic” measure, as AI music made up 43 percent of the tracks distributed to the platform in the last 90 days. “We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all,” Andersen adds.
Bandcamp similarly banned AI music earlier this year, while other music streaming platforms attempt to address a flood of AI songs by applying new labels or removing them from user algorithms. Spotify recently announced that it removed 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from recommendations over the past year, and also launched new “AI persona” badges for artists that use an AI identity. YouTube has rolled out AI music labels as well, while Apple Music is planning to launch AI labels this year. Meanwhile, Deezer is giving users the option to filter out AI music.
“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal says in a separate post on X.
The platform is also going to ban music distributors from submitting AI songs, using the AI detection tool Ircam Amplify and metadata checks to reject submissions generated solely with AI. Tidal notes that it won’t ban songs made with the assistance of AI tools, as long as AI doesn’t make up the “sole output.”

items.title: Why the Premier League's set-piece goals dried up -- and why Arsenal are still No. 1 anyway
items.summary:
Last season, Arsenal scored 19 goals from corner kicks en route to winning their first Premier League title in over 20 years.
You know this because it's all we talked about. And it's all we talked about because (1) Arsenal are one of the most popular sports teams on the planet, and (2) everyone else
items.text:
Last season, Arsenal scored 19 goals from corner kicks en route to winning their first Premier League title in over 20 years.
You know this because it's all we talked about. And it's all we talked about because (1) Arsenal are one of the most popular sports teams on the planet, and (2) everyone else started doing it, too. It became, increasingly, soccer without the soccer.
From one side, bad-faith commentators tried to make it sound like Arsenal's title wasn't worth as much as teams that attacked more aggressively. From the other side, bad-faith commentators acted confused that neutrals didn't enjoy watching a defensive team whose matches featured less ball-in-play time than anyone else in the league.
In the middle: it seemed like modern soccer had reached an inflection point, where a sudden leaguewide strategic shift -- led by the best team in England and one of the three or four best teams in the world -- had made the game worse to watch. That is, if you liked watching things like "passing" and "open-play goals" -- all of them had fallen off a cliff.
Given the vastly different punishments for infractions during a corner kick -- a penalty if a defender is too aggressive, a free kick 100 yards away from goal if the attacker is too aggressive -- teams realized there was little downside to creating what the analyst Michael Caley called a "meat wall" in front of the opposition goalkeeper and grappling for space inside the six-yard box. Teams also seemed to decide, collectively, that there was little upside in taking risks in the other phases of the game.
Had this been the way soccer always worked, then, well, soccer probably never would've become the most popular sport in the world. But any rule-change adopted by the Premier League to make it harder to score from corners would, in a way, be a direct punishment of Arsenal since they drove the shift and they benefitted from it more than anyone.
The Gunners scored just 42 goals from open-play last season and won the title by scoring the most corner kick goals in a season from any Premier League team ever.
With FIFA advising their referees to crack down on penalty-area physicality at the World Cup over the summer, it seemed like set pieces would once again be the story of the Premier League season -- in one way or another.
Well, 11 games into the 2026-27 season, Arsenal have scored just one goal from corner kicks. And Arsenal ... are sitting atop the standings, a full six points clear of second place.
So, we have to ask: What the heck happened?
- Predicting the Premier League season now: How all 20 teams will finish
- Man United need January help to avoid Premier League relegation
- How fallen giants and fans bounce back from scandal and relegation
Why Premier League corner-kick goals are down -- for now
Ahead of this season, the Premier League didn't make any rule changes but instead instructed its referees to focus on "non-footballing holding actions that have no place on the football pitch." This included things like a player not even looking at the ball as he made contact with an opponent or a player making contact with an opponent while not even attempting to make a play on the ball.
These vague directives can often be quite powerful. In 2019, the NFL told refs to stop calling so many holding penalties, the number of holding penalties nearly halved overnight, and it was suddenly easier for offenses to move the ball down the field.
And what do you know? Premier League refs were told to call more fouls during corner kicks, and they are calling more fouls during corner kicks.
Per a study recently conducted by Caley: "Attackers have been called for 5.8 fouls for every 100 corners this season, up from 4.6 last season," It's being driven, in particular, by an increase in fouls suffered by goalkeepers: 3.1 per 100 corners this season, up from 2.5 last season and an average of 1.8 in the five seasons prior.
What happened last season, basically, was that teams packed the six-yard box and then smashed in-swinging corners into that area. In-swingers are much easier to score from because they just require a slight redirection, because they're already headed toward the goal, and because they lead to closer chances to goal than outswingers. Their effectiveness is theoretically canceled out, though, because it's also easier for the goalkeeper to catch them.
The rise in set-piece scoring last season was, essentially, driven by teams realizing there was a way you could hit in-swinging corners and prevent goalkeepers from claiming them. But the increase in foul-calling this season seems to have totally halted the trend.
Here's Caley:
Goalkeeper claims fell to 3.1 per 100 corners taken as crosses last season. This happened even as corner deliveries increasingly targeted areas in the six-yard box where keepers are the most likely to be able to claim the ball. I created a model to predict claims based on where crosses landed, and this model predicted that goalkeepers would be able to catch far more than they actually did, about 7.6 out of every 100 corner crosses. This season the number of claims has nearly doubled, up to 5.6. Punches have been rising, and even continued that trajectory in 2026-27 despite the increase in claims. All told, goalkeepers are now reaching over 15 percent of corner kick crosses.
All of this, unsurprisingly, has tanked the number of goals being scored from corner kicks. The turnaround is remarkable:
We've shifted from one extreme to the other over the course of a single off season. Last season had the highest corner-kick-goal rate of any in the Opta database. This season has the lowest.
Problem solved?
In a sense: yes. We're not talking about how the quality of play is terrible and how we only see set-piece goals anymore. Even with new tactics reshaping the game, the on-field product definitely feels better this season.
But the massive decline in corner-kick goals is likely also a small-sample-size fluke. "While goals from corner kic

items.summary:
Jurrien Timber's shirt-pull on Alexander Isak: Ref chief Howard Webb admits 'quick check' in Arsenal's win at Liverpool
