items.title: 83pc of maternal deaths reviewed linked to delays in hospital care
items.summary:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 24 – Delays in receiving medical attention at health facilities were identified in 83 per cent of maternal deaths reviewed in a Ministry of Health surveillance dataset, exposing persistent gaps in staffing, essential medicines and emergency response in Kenya’s healthcare system.
Th
items.text:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 24 – Delays in receiving medical attention at health facilities were identified in 83 per cent of maternal deaths reviewed in a Ministry of Health surveillance dataset, exposing persistent gaps in staffing, essential medicines and emergency response in Kenya’s healthcare system.
The findings, presented by University of Nairobi researcher Dr Njoki Kimani during a Kenya Editors Guild forum in Nairobi on November 19, point to weaknesses in the quality and timeliness of care even as more women deliver in health facilities.
The analysis also found that 71 per cent of the maternal deaths involved delays in deciding to seek medical attention, highlighting challenges that begin before women reach hospitals.
“We know that 71 per cent of deaths were due to the first delay and 83 per cent were due to delay within the facility,” Kimani said.
The findings examined three categories of delays: deciding to seek medical care, reaching a health facility and receiving appropriate treatment after arrival. Some deaths involved more than one category of delay.
Kimani said postpartum haemorrhage, or excessive bleeding after childbirth, remained the leading cause of maternal deaths in the records examined.
She further revealed that health facilities reporting staff shortages had more than four times the risk of maternal mortality, while shortages of medicines, blood and blood products were also associated with increased risks.
Garissa and Nairobi were among the counties facing significant challenges linked to delays in maternal healthcare. Kimani noted that Nairobi’s facilities also serve patients from neighbouring counties, placing additional pressure on available services.
The findings point to a gap between access to healthcare and the ability of facilities to provide timely, quality emergency treatment.
Medical Services Principal Secretary Dr Ouma Oluga said only 37 per cent of health facilities offering delivery services could provide all seven basic emergency obstetric care functions, raising concerns about their preparedness to manage complications during childbirth.
He urged journalists to investigate weaknesses in maternal healthcare and increase public awareness of preventable deaths.
“Every morning, one minute awareness. It will speak louder than the headlines,” Oluga said, calling on radio and television stations to dedicate daily airtime to maternal and newborn health education.
The Principal Secretary said the government was implementing interventions under the Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere (EWENE) Acceleration Plan to strengthen maternal and newborn healthcare services.
The measures include providing essential medical supplies and obstetric and neonatal equipment to 635 health facilities, establishing training and simulation centres and recruiting an additional 5,000 midwives to address workforce shortages.
Oluga also highlighted the expansion of healthcare coverage under the Social Health Authority (SHA), saying 33.7 million Kenyans had registered under the scheme.
He said the registration data would help improve healthcare planning and resource allocation, while urging expectant mothers to begin antenatal care early, complete the recommended eight visits and attend postnatal appointments.
Kenya Editors Guild President Zubeidah Kananu challenged journalists to sustain coverage of maternal and newborn health beyond individual tragedies, calling for closer scrutiny of government commitments and their implementation.
“We must follow up on promises made, investigate systemic gaps, examine whether interventions are working, and establish whether lessons from previous tragedies are informing better healthcare decisions,” Kananu said.
She cited the September case of Mercy Kanini, a mother from Juja who lost all five of her babies after giving birth prematurely, saying the tragedy raised questions about the management of high-risk pregnancies, access to specialised newborn care and the effectiveness of referral systems.
Kananu said journalists should examine whether lessons from maternal and newborn deaths were being translated into measures that prevent similar tragedies.
She also urged the media to monitor healthcare funding, staffing and the implementation of government programmes to establish whether services promised to expectant mothers were actually available in hospitals.
Dr Wangui Muthigani, Director and Programme Lead for Women’s Health at Savannah Global Health Institute, said maternal mortality statistics should be examined beyond the numbers to understand the circumstances surrounding individual deaths.
She observed that although many pregnant women make initial contact with healthcare facilities, some fail to complete the recommended antenatal visits, resulting in missed opportunities for early diagnosis and intervention.
Muthigani said examining where women drop out of the healthcare system could help identify communities requiring additional support.
“So once we see a mother has died, do we sit and cry? I mean, we should. We should sit and cry, but we should act so that we don’t have a situation like this arising tomorrow,” she said.

“The truest gap is delivery, meaning that the proven tools, the proven interventions are not reaching all the women, and if they are, they’re reaching women a bit too late,” Barsosio said.

items.title: Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
items.summary:
The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.
“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Par
items.text:
The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.
“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”
It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.
That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.
“Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”
Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.
G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.
The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.
“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”
In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.
Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.
“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

items.summary: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and
items.text:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads.
It’s not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Neither Adobe nor the NYT immediately responded to The Verge’s request for more information.

"The world has moved close
items.text:
HIV infections could rise after historic lows amid aid cuts, UN warns
November 24, 2026
New HIV infections could rise next year for the first time in years, reversing a historic decline amid funding cuts and anti-rights campaigns, the United Nations (UN) warned on Tuesday.
"The world has moved closer towards controlling the HIV pandemic, but changes in funding and resulting service disruptions jeopardize this progress," the UNAIDS agency said in its annual global update.
AIDS-related death numbers has fallen to its lowest in more than two decades. According to the organization, this was made possible by broader access to treatment and improvements in the quality of care programs.
The virus claimed roughly 570,000 lives globally in 2025. This means almost 1,600 people died everyday. In comparison, this figure was 600,000 in 2024 and 1.3 million in 2010.
Based on data from 172 countries, the agency estimated that 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV in 2025, of whom 32.1 million were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
The wider use of antiretroviral medication also reduces the risk of HIV transmission, the organization said. It estimates that 1.2 million people contracted HIV in 2025, down from 1.3 million the year before. The peak in 1994 saw 3.5 million.
"HIV, which was once a death sentence, has become a manageable health condition for millions of people thanks to life-saving HIV medicines," said UNAIDS.
'Dramatic impacts' of US aid cuts
Despite the encouraging data so far, cuts to international funding have hampered efforts to fight HIV, the agency warned.
HIV programs faced an 18-percent decrease in international financing over the past year, said UNAIDS.
"Funding losses have destabilized HIV programs worldwide, coinciding with a wider contraction in official development assistance over the years," it said.
Although the United States remains the largest international donor for HIV programs, its contributions dropped by 26% between 2024 and 2025.
After dismantling USAID, the world's largest foreign aid agency, last year, the Donald Trump administration has sought to replace decades of aid with new bilateral deals.
"The impact of the United States government funding cuts has been especially dramatic given the reliance of many countries on its support for core HIV programs," said UNAIDS.
Meanwhile disbursements from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria dropped by 13% in 2025.
Next year's data may show rising infections
"We are on the cusp of ending AIDS – this has been the greatest story of global health – and just when we should finish it, cuts and the rolling back of human rights is threatening to take away our gains," Winnie Byanyima, executive director of UNAIDS, told Reuters.
"We haven't ‌got the data yet, but we see the signs. We see all the signs of reversals," she added.
Byanyima predicted that data released in 2027 would begin to reflect a rise in new HIV infections.
In 2015, the UN set a goal to end AIDS by 2030.

items.title: 2028 Copa América to be played in United States with six Concacaf teams
items.summary:
The 2028 Copa América will be played in the United States and expanded to include teams from the Concacaf region, bringing the landmark South American international competition to the US for a third time in five editions.
Conmebol, the South American confederation that runs the tournament, and Conca
items.text:
The 2028 Copa América will be played in the United States and expanded to include teams from the Concacaf region, bringing the landmark South American international competition to the US for a third time in five editions.
Conmebol, the South American confederation that runs the tournament, and Concacaf, the confederation governing soccer in North and Central America and the Caribbean, jointly announced the long-rumored arrangement on Tuesday, framing it as an extension of a “strategic partnership” between the organizations.
The tournament will be played from 9 June to 9 July 2028 – notably the same dates as Uefa’s European Championship, to be co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland. The 2028 summer Olympics will then follow in venues across the US, with the opening match of the men’s soccer tournament kicking off on 10 July, and the women’s tournament following the next day. The Olympic finals will land on the 28th (men’s) and 29th (women’s) of July.
The 2028 Copa América will involve 16 teams – all of Conmebol’s 10 member nations, along with six from Concacaf. The confederations announced that the Concacaf participants will be determined based on results at the 2027 Gold Cup, set to be played in the US in June and July next year. The exact qualification criteria have yet to be announced.
While the US’s large and growing appetite for soccer is part of the reason it has become a common landing spot for the Copa América over the last decade-plus, commercial considerations will also have been a major factor. The 2024 Copa América, which was also held in the US and involved six Concacaf teams, generated approximately $319m in revenue for Conmebol, the confederation said – a significant rise over the $118m generated by the 2019 edition in Brazil.
Argentina won the 2024 edition of the Copa América, with the final in Miami marred by ugly scenes of ticketless fans rushing the gates, causing injuries and damage to the stadium, delaying the start time by nearly 90 minutes. The previous edition hosted in the US, 2016’s Copa América Centenario, was won by Chile on penalties over Argentina at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
As with that tournament, the 2024 Copa América and the 2026 World Cup, the 2028 tournament can be expected to be played largely in American football stadiums, most with capacities exceeding 60,000 people. But unlike those previous editions, the tournament will not overlap with Major League Soccer, thanks to the US league’s recent calendar flip.

items.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
items.summary: Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether
items.text:
Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos autoplay.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta did when it announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

items.title: Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the gap with Nvidia in the AI chip race
items.summary: Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the r
items.text:
Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

items.title: Manchester United win appeal over Yoro’s one-match suspension after Anfield red card
items.summary:
Manchester United have successfully appealed against the decision to send off Leny Yoro in their 4-0 defeat to Liverpool. The defender was dismissed for denying an obvious goal scoring opportunity after eight minutes but this was found to be incorrect.
The Frenchman will no longer be required to ser
items.text:
Manchester United have successfully appealed against the decision to send off Leny Yoro in their 4-0 defeat to Liverpool. The defender was dismissed for denying an obvious goal scoring opportunity after eight minutes but this was found to be incorrect.
The Frenchman will no longer be required to serve a one-match suspicion. He fouled Liverpool’s Alexander Isak when through on goal in the early stages at Anfield but Mauricio Pochettino insisted the striker would not have reached the ball, and therefore is was not a sending off offence. The referee Sam Barrott made a different assessment, which the video assistant did not disagree with.
United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”
Dominik Szoboszlai scored the resulting free-kick, setting Liverpool on their way to victory to make it a difficult first match in charge for Pochettino. Yoro will now be available to face Brentford on Saturday in the Premier League.

items.title: IEBC powerless to stop early campaigns as AG misses deadline to enact law
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has admitted it has no legal powers to punish politicians conducting premature campaigns ahead of the 2027 General Election, following the failure to enact legislation governing political campaigns.
The commission sa
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 24 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has admitted it has no legal powers to punish politicians conducting premature campaigns ahead of the 2027 General Election, following the failure to enact legislation governing political campaigns.
The commission says it cannot impose sanctions on politicians mobilising support and soliciting votes outside the official campaign period because there is no specific law empowering it to take action against early campaigns.
IEBC officials said the gap persisted despite a High Court directive issued in June 2025 requiring the Attorney General to take steps towards enacting legislation to regulate political campaigns within 12 months.
Speaking during an engagement with journalists, IEBC officials said the court had recognised the dangers posed by premature campaigns but acknowledged that the commission lacked a legal framework through which it could enforce restrictions.
The commission said the absence of legislation left it unable to take punitive action against aspirants already traversing the country, holding political rallies and mobilising supporters ahead of the August 10, 2027 elections.
Mukhwana said the court had ruled that premature political campaigns undermined constitutional principles and fundamental rights, including equality before the law, freedom from violence, impartiality and the right to free and fair elections.
“The court noted that there was no law upon which the IEBC would act,” he said, explaining why the commission could not sanction politicians engaging in early campaigns.
Mukhwana said the June 9, 2025 judgment in Legal Advice Centre t/a Kituo Cha Sheria v IEBC and Others arose from a petition challenging political campaigns conducted before the officially designated election period.
A three-judge bench comprising Justices Hedwig Ong’udi, Patricia Gichohi and Heston Nyaga declared that conducting political campaigns outside the election period violated constitutional principles, including equality, equal protection of the law, freedom from violence, impartiality, the rule of law and the right to free and fair elections.
The judges directed the Attorney General to take the necessary steps within 12 months to enact legislation governing political campaigns conducted outside the official election period.
The deadline expired on June 9, 2026, but IEBC officials said the commission was still without the legislation needed to enforce restrictions on premature campaigns.
Mukhwana said the commission would therefore rely on the existing electoral framework, which provides for the formal campaign period ahead of the 2027 elections.
According to the IEBC’s operational plan, the General Election will be held on August 10, 2027, with the formal campaign period expected to commence after the candidate registration process, which is scheduled to conclude by May 29, 2027.
Campaign financing
IEBC said the commission was also working to enforce the Election Campaign Financing Act, which requires political parties and candidates to comply with prescribed contribution and expenditure limits.
The commission had published campaign financing regulations, contribution limits and spending ceilings, alongside timelines for enforcing the framework.
However, two court cases had complicated implementation, with one filed at the Milimani High Court and another at the Kiambu High Court.
The official said the Kiambu court had issued conservatory orders restraining the commission from enforcing the campaign financing framework.
IEBC subsequently challenged the orders and succeeded in having them vacated last week, with the Kiambu case also transferred to Milimani for consolidation with the existing petition.
The official said the cases were scheduled for mention in February 2027, adding that the absence of restraining orders meant the commission could proceed with enforcement in accordance with its published timelines.
The Election Campaign Financing Act is intended to regulate contributions and expenditure by candidates and political parties, preventing wealthy individuals and organisations from exerting disproportionate influence over electoral competition.
The commission’s attempts to operationalise the framework have previously faced legal and procedural challenges ahead of the 2017 and 2022 elections.
The official also gave an update on procurement disputes involving election technology and ballot papers, saying the commission had faced about eight cases before the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board and the High Court in the past three months.
He said a High Court judgment delivered on Tuesday had dismissed the latest case challenging the election technology procurement process, allowing the evaluation of the tender to proceed.
However, a fresh constitutional petition had been filed immediately after the judgment. The court declined to issue conservatory orders, with the matter scheduled for mention on November 30.
On ballot papers, the official said the remaining case was scheduled for judgment on November 26, expressing hope that its determination would allow the commission to proceed with the procurement process.

items.text:
Players Championship Finals 2026: Schedule and order of play as Gerwyn Price eyes another major title in Minehead
Gerwyn Price looks to back up his Grand Slam of Darts win by claiming a second straight major title; former champions Luke Humphries and Michael van Gerwen also among the 64-player field in Minehead, but world No 1 and defending champion Luke Littler did not qualify
Tuesday 24 November 2026 16:05, UK
The 2026 Ladbrokes Players Championship Finals sees 64 players competing to win the PDC's last major event before the World Darts Championship gets under way in December.
The tournament - which has a newly increased prize fund of £750,000 - features the top 64 ranked players following the conclusion of the 34-event Players Championship season, and takes place at Butlin's Minehead Resort from November 27-29.
Gerwyn Price, recently crowned Grand Slam of Darts champion for a fourth time, opens his bid for back-to-back major titles against Sebastian Bialecki on Friday, with record seven-time winner Michael van Gerwen in action against Connor Scutt and Luke Humphries - triumphant in 2023 and 2024 - going up against Darryl Pilgrim.
Top seed Wessel Nijman has been handed a tough opener against exciting youngster Henry Coates, while Beau Greaves makes her Players Championship Finals debut against Christian Kist.
World No 1 and defending champion Luke Littler did not qualify for the Finals.
Friday's first round winners advance to Saturday's double session, with the second round scheduled for the afternoon and round three in the evening.
The tournament concludes on Sunday November 29, with the afternoon's quarter-finals followed by the semi-finals and final in a decisive evening session that also includes the Winmau World Youth Championship final between Cam Crabtree and Jan Schmidt.

items.title: Kenya Sugar Board aspirant director pledges reforms
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Improved rural roads, cheaper farm inputs, faster-maturing sugarcane varieties and increased financial support are among the priorities Samuel Ongou, one of the aspirants for the Kenya Sugar Board Director position says he will pursue as he seeks to represent the Central Catc
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Improved rural roads, cheaper farm inputs, faster-maturing sugarcane varieties and increased financial support are among the priorities Samuel Ongou, one of the aspirants for the Kenya Sugar Board Director position says he will pursue as he seeks to represent the Central Catchment Area in the Board.
Ongou, who is contesting for the director’s position covering Kisumu, Kericho and Nandi counties, says addressing production challenges and improving farmers’ earnings will be central to his agenda as the sugar industry enters a new phase of reforms.
Speaking as the Kenya Sugar Board elections entered their final stages, Ongou said significant progress had been made in addressing some of the challenges that have troubled sugarcane farmers for years, but maintained that more needed to be done to make the sector sustainable.
He cited the introduction of weekly payments to farmers, clearance of historical arrears and reduction of fertiliser prices as some of the gains achieved under the current administration.
“In the past, there used to be a lot of arrears, particularly from the State-owned mills. Nowadays, all the sugar millers in Kenya are paying weekly,” he said.
Ongou noted that the cost of fertiliser had also been reduced from Sh7,000 to Sh2,000 per 50-kilogramme bag, easing the financial burden on farmers and creating room for increased production.
He further pointed to the ongoing distribution of bonuses as an important intervention in improving farmers’ earnings, noting that President William Ruto had launched the payments in the Nzoia region, with a similar exercise expected in the Central Catchment Area.
However, Ongou said poor road infrastructure remained one of the major obstacles affecting sugarcane production, particularly in areas where farmers struggle to transport mature cane to milling factories.
He pledged to prioritise road rehabilitation and ensure funds allocated for infrastructure development were utilised to improve access to farms and facilitate timely cane delivery.
“We will make sure that the roads are fixed. We will also make sure that we roll out money for cane development to farmers, which will be at three per cent,” he said.
Another key area he wants addressed is the development of early-maturing sugarcane varieties, which he believes could transform productivity and profitability in the region.
Ongou said the Kenya Sugar Research and Training Institute (KESRETI) had received funding to prepare planting materials for improved varieties expected to mature within nine to 12 months.
He contrasted the proposed varieties with existing ones, including Company 617, which takes at least 18 months to mature, saying shorter maturity periods would enable farmers to harvest more frequently.
The development, he said, would help farmers improve their annual production cycles, increase income and reduce the time and resources spent maintaining their crops before harvesting.
“We want to make sure that farmers in the coming future will be harvesting yearly, compared to the current varieties which take at least 18 months and above. The new varieties will be between nine and 12 months,” he said.
Ongou expressed confidence that continued investment in research, infrastructure and farmer support would help restore the competitiveness of the sugar industry and make cane farming a commercially viable enterprise.
He also called for unity among farmers and candidates, urging them to maintain peace as the election process concludes.
He said leadership should be viewed as an opportunity to serve all farmers regardless of their political or regional affiliations, adding that divisions would only undermine efforts to address challenges in the sector.
“We are one Kenya. Once elected, I will serve everybody. I don’t see why we need to fight,” he said.
Ongou said his focus would be on consolidating the gains already made while pushing for practical interventions that directly improve the livelihoods of sugarcane farmers across the Central Catchment Area.

items.text:
Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling
- Published
Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).
The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.
The result of that match in Rabat, which saw the Teranga Lions triumph 1-0 after extra time, was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed Senegal had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to Cas, sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.
In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners.
The court said it considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."
The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always".
Caf is yet to comment on the decision but its president Patrice Motsepe has repeatedly said that his organisation will respect and adhere to the Cas ruling.
Morocco's football federation (FRMF) is also yet to comment on the verdict.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final 
  - Published19 January
Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.
This ruling should now settle any debate about who the history books will recognise as continental champions - although plenty in Morocco may not agree with the outcome of the case at Cas.
What happened in the Afcon final?
A tightly-contested match between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Jean-Jacques Ndala at the centre of the drama.
First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.
The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.
Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Brahim Diaz back before heading a corner clear.
Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by VAR.
Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.
They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.
The game went into extra time, with midfielder Pape Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.
But, off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.
What was the fallout?
Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.
It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".
A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's protest days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.
Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.
The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.
The director general of the Switzerland-based court said arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.
The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.
The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.
Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.
But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 24 – Some 4.5 million regular borrowers under the Hustler Fund are set to benefit from enhanced credit limits, with eligible individuals now able to access loans of up to KSh150,000 through the bridge loan facility.
President William Ruto announced the changes on Tuesday, alongside an additional KSh5 billion allocation to the Government-backed credit programme.
Ruto said the increased funding is intended to address the inadequacy of resources available to borrowers and ensure more Kenyans can access affordable financing.
The enhanced borrowing limits will target regular borrowers through the bridge loan facility, allowing them to access higher amounts to support their financial needs and economic activities.
The President also directed the Hustler Fund management to develop a group financing product that will enable organised groups to borrow and determine how to lend the money to individual members.
The proposed arrangement is expected to give groups greater flexibility in accessing credit and distributing funds according to members’ needs.
Ruto made the announcements during the 17th anniversary celebrations of the Joyful Women Organisation at State House, Nairobi.
The event was attended by First Lady Rachel Ruto, the organisation’s patron, and Deputy President Kithure Kindiki.
The latest interventions are part of the Government’s efforts to widen access to affordable credit, particularly among individuals and groups seeking financing outside conventional lending arrangements.

items.text:
Millwall face partial stadium closure over chants
- Published
Millwall have been ordered to play a future Championship match in front of a partially-closed stadium as punishment for fans' discriminatory chants.
The club has also been fined £70,000 by an independent regulatory commission, and been told another offence this season will lead to a further partial stadium closure.
The sanctions were imposed for ableist and homophobic chants, heard at a game against Charlton Athletic in January.
"These chants are discriminatory, unacceptable, and will not be tolerated at The Den or anywhere Millwall play," Millwall's managing director Mark Fairbrother said in an open letter to supporters., external
"The club condemns them without reservation. They do not represent this club, and the vast majority of supporters who follow Millwall home and away with passion and pride.
"Incidents like this hurt all of us, but none more so than people who are directly discriminated against by ableist, homophobic or other unacceptable chanting, and we apologise to anybody that was affected, offended or impacted by the chants."
Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand - the two-tiered east stand at The Den - will have to be closed for the Championship fixture against Sheffield United on 8 December.
It is the first time a club has been given this level of sanction for discriminatory chanting, with the commission saying "the club's previous disciplinary record was a significant aggravating feature".
'This is a serious outcome'
The commission pointed to chants relating to race in a 2019 fixture against Everton, religion in a 2023 fixture away at Wigan Athletic, and sexual orientation and disability in a 2025 visit to Crystal Palace, all of which resulted in fines for the club.
"History has shown that combinations of action plans and fines have been wholly ineffective to prevent the club - through its supporters - committing breaches" of Football Association (FA) rules around discriminatory behaviour, the commission added.
The FA had charged Millwall in March for the chanting against Charlton.
The club admitted the charge, and in its submissions suggested the chants were limited to 80 to 100 individuals in the north-eastern corner of the Dockers Stand, in the blocks that will be closed as part of the punishment.
However, based on other evidence, the commission concluded the actual figure involved in the chants was "likely to have been in the hundreds, quite possibly more".
It also found that the club did not make any announcement over the stadium PA system ordering for the discriminatory chanting to stop, nor did it deploy any additional stewards or police to the areas from where the chanting was originating.
"I won't dress this up. This is a serious outcome," Fairbrother said.
"This significant sanction was given because, although this is the first charge relating to a match at The Den for many years, the commission took into account a number of incidents of discriminatory chanting involving our supporters over the past few seasons at away games.
"This is the cumulative cost of that pattern. Most importantly, the current and any future sanctions mean the next incident won't just cost the club money. It will cost supporters their seats.
"Innocent fans will be shut out of their own stadium because of someone else's behaviour, and with future sanctions likely to be tougher, that threat is very real."

items.title: Senegal restored as Africa Cup of Nations champions after court ruling
items.summary:
Senegal have been restored as the Africa Cup of Nations champions after a ruling by the court of arbitration for sport (Cas).
Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in a chaotic Afcon final in January but the result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by
items.text:
Senegal have been restored as the Africa Cup of Nations champions after a ruling by the court of arbitration for sport (Cas).
Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in a chaotic Afcon final in January but the result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (Caf).
Senegal appealed and on Tuesday Cas published the verdict of its panel of three judges.
The three-person panel came to their decision unanimously, deciding that the field of play doctrine which decrees that any referee’s decision is final must ultimately hold sway.
“After having examined the arguments raised by the Parties, the Arbitral Panel considered that the Referee’s decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority,” a Cas statement said. “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met.
“In the Panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee’s decision were limited to the pitch. As such, the Panel considers that the Referee’s decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine.”
Claims by the Royal Moroccan Football Federation that Senegal had contravened articles of the Afcon Regulations, were rejected by the panel. “Since Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations are intended solely to determine the outcome of a match when a team’s conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently, they are therefore not applicable in this case.”
During the final, Senegal beat Morocco in Rabat after causing a 15-minute delay in play when they walked off in protest at Morocco being awarded a penalty in the last minute of normal time.
Senegal’s star forward Sadio Mané helped to persuade his team to return as tensions rose in the stadium and when the referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala, restarted the game, Morocco’s Brahim Díaz had his penalty saved. Senegal won with a Pape Gueye goal in extra time.
Football’s laws state that referee decisions are final but Caf appeal judges cited Afcon tournament regulations that if a team “refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition”.
The Cas judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing. Cas verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland’s supreme court, though only on limited procedural grounds.
More than $1m (£770,000) in fines were imposed by Caf disciplinary judges on the two federations, players and Senegal’s then coach, Pape Thiaw.

items.text:
Senegal crowned AFCON 2025 champions by Court of Arbitration for Sport following appeal
An announcement confirmed CAS determined Senegal to be the winners of the tournament, which concluded in January; Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in the final, but were stripped of the title in March, which led to their appeal
Tuesday 24 November 2026 14:30, UK
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) have announced Senegal as the winners of AFCON 2025.
Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 in the final in January, but were stripped of the title by a Confederation of African Football (CAF) Appeal Board in March for breaking competition rules by walking off the pitch because of a late disallowed goal and a controversial penalty award.
Senegal's protest caused a delay of 15 minutes, and when their players returned to the pitch, Morocco's Brahim Diaz missed the penalty to force the match into extra time.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025)," a CAS statement read.
"The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 for Senegal)."
Morocco's appeal was initially rejected but a CAF panel did uphold it and found Senegal's walk-off meant they had forfeited the match, awarding a 3-0 win to Morocco.
Senegal then appealed to CAS, calling the decision "a travesty," and have now been reinstated as champions.
Morocco's initial appeal was rejected but a CAF panel did uphold it and found Senegal's walk-off meant they had forfeited the match, awarding a 3-0 win to Morocco.
CAF said Senegal infringed on article 82 of AFCON's regulations, which states if a team refuses to play or leaves the ground before the end of regulation time without the refereee's authorisation, it will be considered the loser and eliminated from the competition.
Article 84 states any team that violates article 82 will be permanently eliminated and lose the match 3-0.
Senegal then appealed to CAS, calling the decision "a travesty," and have now been reinstated as champions.
'Common sense prevails' but is this really over?
Sky Sports News' Chief Correspondent Kaveh Solhekol:
"Common sense has prevailed because the Court of Arbitration for Sport have effectively confirmed that Senegal did win the 2025 AFCON.
"Morocco were very unhappy because they felt that the rules of the tournament had been broken by Senegal when they left the pitch. They felt that at that stage Senegal should have forfeited the game.
"They went to the African Confederation Appeal Board and there was an appeal hearing in March. That appeal decided that yes, Morocco were right and they should be the winners and the result of the game was changed from a 1-0 win to Senegal to a 3-0 win to Morocco.
"Then we had the next chapter in this story because Senegal were also very unhappy with the decision of the appeal board, so they went to CAS in Switzerland. There was a hearing in October and now we have had the decision - a unanimous decision from the three judges.
"I don't want to tempt fate, because let's wait and see what the Moroccan Federation say, but what I would say to you is that they have fought this all the way, they believe that this is an injustice and they are one of the most powerful football associations in Africa.
"They are co-hosts of the next World Cup in 2030 and they have a very close relationships with the leadership at FIFA.
"I'm not suggesting that anything untoward is going on, but they still do have options. For instance, if they feel there has been something wrong in the procedures at the CAS hearing, they could go to the Swiss Federal Tribunal.
"I think the Moroccan Federation, according to what Reuters are reporting this afternoon, are unhappy with the way CAS handled this appeal and they have complained to CAS because they believe that one of the judges actually spoke on the phone to the president of the Senegal Federation on Sunday afternoon, so perhaps that is an avenue that they are going to explore."
'Unanimous decision' - CAS statement in full
The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025).
The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 for Senegal).
The FSF appealed to CAS against a decision of the CAF Appeal Board declaring that the Senegal national team forfeited the AFCON 2025 final and recording the Moroccan national team as the winners.
In their appeal, the FSF argued that the decision of the Referee, Mr Jean-Jacques Ngambo Ndala, to resume the match at the 109th minute (90+19) during the AFCON 2025 final and to allow it to be concluded with a sporting result could not be reviewed, pursuant to the 'field of play' doctrine.
The FRMF argued, on the contrary, that the Referee's decision did not fall under the 'field of play' doctrine, as it cannot be applicable to the disciplinary consequences of the Senegalese team's behaviour. The FRMF alleged that, by leaving the pitch temporarily, the Senegalese team breached Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON Regulations, which should have led the Referee to bring the match to an early conclusion. The FRMF also argued that the Referee erred in law and that his decision was arbitrary.

items.summary:
Millwall forced to partially close the Den after commission proves FA charges of discriminatory chanting
Millwall have been punished for discriminatory chanting relating to disability and sexual orientation by fans in a game against Charlton in January; a two-game partial stadium closure (one game o
items.text:
Millwall forced to partially close the Den after commission proves FA charges of discriminatory chanting
Millwall have been punished for discriminatory chanting relating to disability and sexual orientation by fans in a game against Charlton in January; a two-game partial stadium closure (one game of which is suspended) is first of its kind at this level; Millwall also fined £70,000
Tuesday 24 November 2026 14:04, UK
Millwall have become the first club in the top four divisions of English football to be punished with a partial stadium closure for discriminatory chanting after a regulatory commission proved two FA charges.
The unprecedented measure is for Millwall failing to ensure their supporters didn't engage in discriminatory chanting that includes reference to disability and sexual orientation during a home match with Charlton in January.
As well as a two-game partial stadium closure - one game of which is suspended until the end of the 2027/28 season - Millwall have been fined £70,000 plus hearing costs, warned about their future conduct, and have had their FA Action Plan extended until the end of next season.
Blocks 19, 20, 47 and 48 of the Dockers Stand will be closed when Millwall host Sheffield United on December 8 - a total of 1,274 seats.
In their written conclusions, the commission found "the club's degree of culpability in relation to the incidents was significant".
In response, speaking exclusively to Sky Sports, Millwall managing director Mark Fairbrother said: "As a club, we didn't do enough and on behalf of the club I apologise to everyone who has been affected by that chanting because it shouldn't happen."
Millwall pleaded guilty to the charges but Fairbrother said Millwall were "disappointed" with the outcome.
He also pointed to new processes the club have since put in place to try to avoid a recurrence - but called on other football clubs, the FA, and organisations such as Kick It Out to come together to find preventative solutions.
"We challenge everything we do and look at if there are ways that we can improve? It's highlighted where we need to be better," he said. "We had already put mitigations in place and need to continue to do so.
"But this is one football club. These instances are happening across football. This is a challenge for the sport in general.
"We see it this [past] week with the charges to Chelsea and also the FA for the England fans in Spain. So, we can put measures in place but we're one club. We can't solve all of society's issues.
"We need to work with all key football stakeholders to look at how can we all do this better? What does good look like? What does best practice look like? And making sure that we embrace that. But everyone else has a collective responsibility as well."
'Focus must be on fan education'
Fairbrother says "the stick approach" used against clubs whose supporters are found guilty of discriminatory chanting just "punishes the fans who actually are just here to enjoy themselves". Instead, he asks "what can we do in terms of the carrot approach to educate people to eradicate this?"
He also noted that supporters identified in the discriminatory chanting against Charlton were all under 18 years old.
"That shows a lack of understanding of the implication of these words," he said. "These words obviously hurt and they have a significant impact on those groups that it affects. But there's that lack of understanding of the issue and the impact."
Asked if he would be interested in working more with groups such as Kick It Out to address this aspect, Fairbrother said: "I'd embrace it. From a personal perspective, I think that would be really good and I implore them to please come work with us, come and look at what we do, challenge what we do.
"If you don't think something we're doing is good enough, come and tell us but look at solutions. If we all have a solutions-focused mindset, we can actually start to make real difference."
The regulatory commission also wrote in their conclusions that "the reputation of the club and English football would have been tarnished" by the chanting during a game shown live on Sky Sports. Fairbrother feels that.
"It hurts all of us in the club. But I know it hurts our fans as well because that is not who we are," he said.
Millwall play Charlton again at the Den on December 19 in a Championship fixture. On how the club are working to avoid a repeat of the discriminatory chanting heard in January, Fairbrother said: "We've put in place a number of procedures already.
"We've already had West Ham here earlier in the season, which was probably our highest-risk fixture for a number of years. That went without incident. But we had a different approach to different fan groups in terms of just reminding them of their responsibility.
"But also for us as a club, making sure that we're on the front foot in terms of everything we do. We will have that same approach to Charlton. You can't predict the future, but we have a more robust process in place now."
This latest issue was the first case of discriminatory chanting at the Den since an FA Cup tie with Everton in 2019 - but follows three other cases involving Millwall supporters away from home since April 2023.
Asked whether he is confident of making a difference, Fairbrother said that would require the support of Millwall fans to call out discriminatory language.
"For each of those instances - and all three of them were away games - there were specific small fan groups who obviously engaged with that chanting. This is now the first instance we've had here at the Den," he said.
"So for all fans, we need to check and challenge this. We need to make sure it doesn't build up. Don't engage with this type of chanting.
"It's not fair on [other Millwall supporters]. We need to all do better. As a club, we need to do better and we will do better for them. But also, it's a collective one. If it happens, if people see it, call it out. We all need to be more proactive on this.

items.title: ‘I’m loving it at Brugge’: Freddie Potts on going from West Ham’s bench to Champions League
items.summary: In April Freddie Potts was absorbing the disappointment of being substituted at half-time during West Ham’s FA Cup quarter-final defeat by Leeds. The midfielder was out of favour under Nuno Espírito Santo and could not have imagined that he would be preparing to face Liverpool in the Champions Leagu
items.text:
In April Freddie Potts was absorbing the disappointment of being substituted at half-time during West Ham’s FA Cup quarter-final defeat by Leeds. The midfielder was out of favour under Nuno Espírito Santo and could not have imagined that he would be preparing to face Liverpool in the Champions League seven months later.
It is the 23-year-old’s reward for taking the difficult decision to leave his boyhood club last summer. Potts noticed his minutes were drying up in pre-season, even though West Ham were not exactly stocked with talent after relegation, and was ready for a new challenge when Club Brugge offered about £10m to sign him.
“I thought this was the perfect place for me to take the next step,” Potts says of his move to the Belgian champions. “I’m not going to shy away – it was very hard. West Ham have been my club for my whole life. I still have a lot of love for West Ham. But I had to take into account what was best for my career and I’m loving it at Brugge.
“Every player wants to be in the team expected to win every week, and seeing how Club Brugge have performed in the Champions League before shows the project and how they want to develop the team and players. It was a very exciting place for me to come. They look to develop young players.”
Potts was six when he joined West Ham. His father, Steve, made 506 appearances for the club and is part of Scott Parker’s backroom staff there. His brother, Dan, came through the academy before moving to Luton in 2015. This is a West Ham family; it is not a surprise that moving to Belgium was emotional for Potts.
Yet it was the right move. Brugge are second in the Belgian Pro League, a point behind Union Saint-Gilloise, and have impressed in the Champions League. They have nine points from four games in the league phase and caused a stir when they beat Inter 4-3 at San Siro last month.
Potts calls it “one of the best nights of my career”. It was quite the turnaround for a player who mostly watched from the bench as West Ham tried to save themselves during the second half of last season. It helps that Potts knows how to stay calm. He was talked up as a future West Ham captain when he made his full debut and impressed in a 3-1 win over Newcastle last year. He had a run in the team but lost his place when Nuno switched to a 4-4-2 in January and settled on Mateus Fernandes and Tomas Soucek as his preferred partnership in central midfield.
That was when Potts remembered how he grew during loan spells at Portsmouth and Wycombe. “I know that you can have games where you feel like you are on top of the world, and then you can come straight back down,” he says. “The loans helped me out massively with West Ham because I managed to cope with the highs. The Newcastle game was a real high, but there were some lows after that and I feel like I was coping with it.”
Potts saw the reaction on social media when he left. Some West Ham fans were not happy with the club for allowing a homegrown player to depart. This season has been tough for West Ham, who are ninth in the Championship after a disappointing run and replaced Nuno with Parker this month. One problem has been the absence of a No 6. Potts, who can snap into a tackle and link play from deep, has been watching from afar.
“I still think they’re playing well,” he says. “They’ve got a great team, great players. I think Scott Parker is a really good manager and he’s got three teams promoted from the Championship. I don’t think it will be a problem again. West Ham will get promoted in the end.”
Potts has glitzier assignments and is adjusting to his surroundings. He cannot speak much Flemish but he has sipped a couple of Belgian beers and is enjoying life in Bruges. “I’m not going to lie, when I first joined I found it difficult. It’s completely different when you move country. But I was open to the challenge. At the start it was a challenge but now it’s really smooth.”
One of the biggest challenges has been adapting to a new style. Given the intensity of the Premier League it is a surprise to hear Potts say Brugge, managed by the 48-year-old Croatian Ivan Leko, have helped him become more physical.
“Straight away in training programmes it was a real surprise how hard everyone works,” Potts says. “It’s in the nature of the club to really work hard and give 100% every day. You see that straight away as you come in the door. No matter how hard it can be everyone gets on with it. No complaints. We’re a running team and everyone gives it their all. That’s the message from the top. It’s a real positive environment for someone of my age to be part of.”
Brugge have a couple of rising stars in attack: the rapid Portugal winger Carlos Forbs and the 22-year-old striker Nicolò Tresoldi, who scored a hat-trick in the win over Inter. There is a feeling Leko’s side could go on a run in Europe. They do not fear Liverpool. “It’ll be difficult for them coming to our place,” Potts says. “They’re a great team but we’re going to approach it like we have been doing with every game.
“Inter are one of the top teams in the competition. PSV are a great team and we got the win there. Liverpool will be tough but we’ve proved it against top teams before.”

Tuesday 24 November 2026 13:00, UK
Nottinghamshire have announced the signing of England bowler Ollie Robinson on a three-year all-format deal.
The signing signals the end of an 11-year spell for Robinson at Sussex - whom he captained during the 2026 County Championship Division One season - despite having a year left on his contract.
Robinson joins the 2025 Division One title winners with a stellar first-class record of 520 wickets at an average of 21.09, while boasting 104 wickets at an average of 19.25 for England's Test side.

items.text:
Imane Khelif still set for professional contest in Paris on December 15 despite withdrawal of original opponent
Imane Khelif was the subject of a fierce gender eligibility row at the Olympic Games; she hasn't boxed since winning gold at Paris 2024; Algerian is due to fight as a professional in Paris on December 15
Tuesday 24 November 2026 13:04, UK
Imane Khelif is still set to box for the first time since the Olympic Games even though her scheduled opponent has withdrawn.
Algeria's Khelif won Olympic welterweight gold in Paris in 2024, while a fierce gender eligibility row overshadowed her participation.
Khelif was cleared to compete by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), despite the International Boxing Association (an organisation that itself has been banned from Olympic boxing) having banned her from the previous year's World Championships for allegedly failing to meet gender eligibility criteria.
Khelif hasn't boxed since beating Liu Yang in that Olympic final, but is due to have a professional bout in Paris on December 15.
That fight next month will go ahead although Khelif's original opponent Clarida Sarabia has withdrawn and Khelif is now looking for a replacement.
"The opponent did have to withdraw from the fight for administrative reasons," a spokesperson for promoter Stair Event told Reuters.
"But the bout is still scheduled for December 15. We'll announce the opponent soon."
In February, Khelif said she was open to genetic testing only if administered by the IOC.

items.text:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
5 min read
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?
Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.
So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.
It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks
Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.
So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???
This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!
Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.
Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.
And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.
This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.
On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.
- And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi broke more records on Tuesday as the 15-year-old cricket sensation guided India A to a seven-wicket win vs UAE with an extraordinary knock; the opener made an asto
items.text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi smashes fastest hundred and double century in List A cricket during India A's victory over UAE
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi broke more records on Tuesday as the 15-year-old cricket sensation guided India A to a seven-wicket win vs UAE with an extraordinary knock; the opener made an astounding 204 runs off a mere 53 deliveries, including 28 sixes,
Tuesday 24 November 2026 13:10, UK
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has broken more records as the teenage cricket sensation smashed his way to the fastest century and double century in List A cricket during India A's seven-wicket victory against the United Arab Emirates on Tuesday.
The 15-year-old produced an extraordinary innings, making 204 off a mere 53 deliveries, including 28 sixes, during the Asia Cup Rising Stars group match in Doha.
Sooryavanshi, who became the youngest debutant for India's senior T20 side in July, first raced his way to a 28-ball century, the fastest ton hit in List A cricket, surpassing Jake Fraser-McGurk by one delivery.
- Sooryavanshi becomes youngest player to debut for India
- Who are Sooryavanshi's rivals for world's best T20 opener?
- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
The Indian prodigy then went one better, advancing to his second ton off 24 balls to obliterate the record, previously held by Chad Bowes, for the fastest double century struck in List A cricket [103 balls].
His 40-ball 150 was also the fastest in List A cricket too, with the 15-year-old going on to smash four consecutive sixes.
It came after UAE had set India a target of 250 to win and thanks to Sooryavanshi's feats, Tilak Varma's side would go on to seal victory inside 14.2 overs.
Sooryavanshi completed the feat by smashing an incredible 28 sixes and seven fours, with a strike rate of 384.90.
That surpassed Western Australia's D'Arcy Short's record tally of 23 maximums, which he managed during a match against Queensland in 2019.
Known as a ruthless ball striker, Sooryavanshi was named the IPL's MVP for the 2026 season, after leading the league with 776 runs and a strike rate of 237.30.
In February, he set a new record for the highest score made at an Under-19 Cricket World Cup final, making 175 runs from 80 deliveries, as India went on to seal a 100-run win against England.
Sooryavanshi would ultimately be dismissed in the 13th over after he clipped a delivery from Basil Hameed to Aryansh Sharma at long-off.
